Today I'll provide an overview of Fairfax County's tax relief program for seniors and people with disabilities and I'll include with the observations that we've made by this analysis and happy to answer any questions.

As part of the FI27 budget guidance, the board asked staff to evaluate the county's senior tax relief program following several enhancements that the county's made over the past few years. Specifically, the board requested an analysis of comparable programs, participation, and utilization trends, whether they're effectively reaching the intended beneficiaries.

As you can see on this slide, we have the agenda for this presentation that I'll be going through. It covers the current program, the analysis of the other jurisdictions, growth in our disabled veteran tax exemption, implementation considerations, and the discussion.

These are the current program limitations for senior tax relief here in Fairfax County. relief ranges from 100% as you see there on the slide for $60,000 and less to 25% up to $90,000 on the gross income. The changes that were approved in 2021 began in 2022 tax year, which was where we increased the gross income limitation from 72,000 to 90,000. for relief, along with the tax deferral. This just provides an income distribution of the applicants on the program. same distribution here for the net financial worth and or your asset qualifications as it states and shows there on the slides. So we provide the largest overall dollar amount in tax relief we also rank near the top when you compare the amount relieved in total to our real estate tax base this is only

looking into tax relief for seniors and people with disabilities it's not any of the other programs we administer in this office with such as our disabled veterans and our surviving spouse exemptions here you're seeing a comparable of our tax deferral program along with the other neighboring jurisdictions that have it. So it's to be mindful that not all offer this tax deferral program.

The participation remains low. I mean, this is our, you know, since 2023, we've had this program and you're not seeing a large number of participants contributing and taking part in this program. This slide is indicating the disabled veteran tax exemption. That's not the purpose of this hearing, but it is to provide you clarification on what my office oversees and handles. We oversee the senior program along with this program. So the growth in the senior and the growth in the veterans contributes to additional administrative burden and the need for additional staff.

Timeline. So tax relief for seniors, we're running on a calendar on the tax year. So we're going to be mailing out our applications for this upcoming year in January. Because of that, we need to look at adopting a year in advance any changes so we can make any necessary changes technology-wise or staffing-wise. At this point, that concludes what I have on our tax relief program, and I'm open for any questions. Thank you very much for that presentation. I appreciate the data, and we're going to have some decisions to make moving forward. I know what the time crunch is for this budget, but I think for out-year budgets, you know, this should be a consideration. It is nice to know that we're competitive with some of the other jurisdictions around here, but I do think there's still some improvements that can be made to this. I guess the only question I have is your, when you look

at FY23 to 26 and you look at the total number of participants in the senior and disabled tax relief program, I think it's fair to say that's a pretty flat number over those four years. And so Is it your professional opinion that we probably have plateaued in terms of the number of applicants?

Or are you looking at this data differently than kind of the raw numbers that appear on the chart? So, one, we keep tax relief open in Fairfax County for the current year and immediately prior. So we're still processing last year's tax relief. These numbers are still going to grow along with this year.

In regards to it, I can't really say if it was a plateau. But, I mean, we are estimating in the demographics report a growth in the senior population. So, over these upcoming years, we should see a trend in growth in the program just based on an increasing number of seniors in the county.

Okay. And I think that's one of the things we need to be watching carefully because, you know, from my standpoint, I think when we did expansions of the program, probably expected the number to grow. So I'm not sure this matched what I think some of our expectations would be.

And I'm understanding, especially the FY26 number is not complete. I get that. The only other thing I would say is, and it's a prickly subject, and I appreciate that you included it in here, for folks watching the Disabled Veteran Exemption Program, which is a good program, is approved and required by Virginia Code.

So that was a program approved by the Virginia General Assembly, not by the Board of Supervisors. And I know there's been a number of conversations, especially at VACO and some other organizations, about the state understanding what the revenue impact is to localities of this program.

And some of the numbers are daunting. And, again, it's a good program. But when you look at the fiscal impact of the Disabled Veteran Exemption Program, The fiscal impact of that program is larger than the fiscal impact of the entire senior and disabled real estate tax relief program that is set and administered by Fairfax County.

So I do think this is something that the Virginia General Assembly is going to have to look at, and it may be a very good program, but I think our strategy in the past always has been the Virginia General Assembly proposes this. They should have found a way to make localities whole because this number of $65 million is a player and driver in what we're able to do to expand the senior and disabled tax relief program.

You have to look at those in totality to understand what the revenue impact is. And so I appreciate that you included that slide, even though it's not directly responsive to the question that you were asked. But it does paint the whole picture, I think, very clearly. So appreciate the information.

Obviously, this is something that as the Budget Committee, as we progress through future budgets, this is something we have to be aware of and be looking at and make sure that we're doing everything we can. You know, there is nothing I hear about more from our senior population than concerns about real estate tax bills.

And so that's not going away. And it's something that we're going to have to continue to address. Questions from board members on the presentation? Supervisor Behrman. Thank you. So, I mean, in regards to it, individuals prefer relieving of the taxes over the deferral. So that obviously plays into part of it. Well, yes, of course. That taxes and not liking to pay taxes are the only things that we all, you know, agree on.

In regards to it, though, one thing that is a big factor into this, lean against the property. So we have many homeowners who have liens against the property still.

Unfortunately, unless the lender agrees to that, we're not going to be able to defer the taxes. So that's a big contributing factor. I mean, we have, you see there on the slide, our interest rate. It's adjusted based on the Wall Street Journal prime rate.

So whether or not the board would like to consider a flat rate and possibly bringing that down, that would be to the discretion of the board. But well, candidly, the legislator will remain nameless, but very few times have I had somebody from Richmond call me up literally about 19 hours ago and say, hey, what do you think if I put in a bill about, you know, being able to put a lien on your property, but defer your taxes?

Do you think that would work? And I said, actually, we have that program and nobody uses it. And I've never had I mean, it was like almost a Marshall McLuhan type moment there. So thank you, and it would be interesting to think about what could be done on that front, given the questions that we get asked.

Thank you. And I think on that front, Jimmy, the recommendation of going to deferred interest rate of zero hasn't moved the needle in those other jurisdictions. I mean, in northern Virginia, there's 27 people who are using it because it was zero and maybe not because it was zero. And so I don't know that that's the remedy.

Correct. Appreciate the comment. Other questions board members have? Yep. Supervisor Herity. On slide 10, and again, the biggest problem I hear is more the net worth limit outside the principal residence. I was just looking at Loudon, and you've got an asterisk that they've got a sliding sale, but they go up to one. How does their sliding scale work?

So they provide different percentages of relief depending on where your income and the net financial worth falls. So someone may have assets of, let's say, $750,000, but based on their income, they can fall in different thresholds. Similar to us, how we have the $175,000, $50,000, and $25,000.

Okay. Are we aware, are any jurisdictions in Virginia that exempt a portion of 401k? To my knowledge, no. So nobody's doing that. Because, you know, we encourage people to put away to save for their retirement, and that's what they're going to live on if they don't have a pension.

So you can't afford to live here on Social Security. I mean, it's pretty simple that that doesn't work. So if you've got your big 401K, but it's not huge, but it's enough to supplement you while you stay here, To me, that's something that at some point in time I'd love to figure out.

Are we allowed to do that? Do we know? Is the state allowed? Yeah. Dan Robinson is here, but my understanding, Mr. Chairman Jay Dilshie, the DTA, my understanding is the board has flexibility. The state controlled every aspect of it, and I believe that if the board so chose, it could go in that direction.

Yeah, and what I would envision, just as a financial guy, would be if you were to take a certain amount at a certain age and convert it to an annuity, you'd exclude that amount if it still kept them below the income level. But that gets really complicated. And I'd love to see your guys that already have trouble with these seniors try to explain that. But that would, to me, be fair for people that, because if you've got a pension payment, as many of our government workers do, that amount, as long as it keeps you below the

income threshold you're good you know or if you're a teacher a retired county employee but if if um if you've saved through 401k you're you're kind of out of luck on until your assets are gone and then mr chairman superintendent you're absolutely correct the challenge as you know is even if you attempt to go out and buy an annuity in the open market the current interest rates are going to determine how much you get for the same sum of money yeah when money was cheap at two percent 2.25% on prime rate.

You've got a lot more than you do today with 7% Wall Street Journal prime rate. Yeah, I think we need to do something there on the asset limit at some time. That's where I would focus the effort. That's my two cents.

Appreciate that. Okay. Supervisor Stork. Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I know we've all been hearing, and particularly when I go to regional meetings, I hear a lot about the Civil Veteran Exemption Program and its impact on counties broadly.

And I know for us, maybe percentage-wise, it doesn't have the same impact that they may be having to staff, et cetera. But obviously, for us, it's a significant amount of dollars. Mr. Chairman the board has been on record for all tax relief programs that represent mandates That the board would prefer that there is 100% reimbursement by the Commonwealth So I think that we've been able to leverage that position as we make the board's position known

Virginia tax just completed a workgroup study on the disabled veterans program And while there's a variety of discussions and a recognition that this is, the program is exploding way beyond what anyone expected, I think the challenges coming up with legislative fixes, even as the Commonwealth has surpluses and the local governments are, some jurisdictions report up to 8% of the general fund revenues being consumed by this program.

To your point, if we're seeing it, the growth slowing down at all, right now, no. We're projecting just by 2028 we'll be in excess of $100 million in real estate tax revenue just for the disabled veteran exemption.

Wow, I did not appreciate that. I mean, to me, seeing the number of $65 million today, I don't know that was in my head before this. I'm not addressing the issue of… Right. Even today, the combined impact, and soon to grow, of course, as we get more applications even for tax year 25, the combined impact of these two programs is almost $110 million between the traditional tax relief and the veterans program.

Agenda item two is administration of a tax rebate. Christina, do you want to kick that off again? Yeah, so for this presentation, it's going to be led by both Jay Doshi and Greg Brook from the Department of Tax Administration. Mr. Chairman, Greg, all yours.

Good morning, Mr. Chairman, members of the board. My name is Greg Brook. I am the deputy director of the Department of Tax Administration. The presentation we have for you today is regarding the board matter requesting analysis of a potential tax rebate. So, as you see here, the board matter requested that we analyze administration options, personnel and operational costs, pros, cons, and ordinance requirements.

For some background, Virginia Code 15.2-2511.1 provides the authority for localities to return surplus funds. We will go into more details on the restrictions and requirements based on the statute in the next slide. We also wanted to provide a brief overview of other localities in Virginia that have adopted ordinances and issued rebates under this authority.

Those localities are the counties of Chesterfield, Henrico, and Louisa, and the city of Richmond. All four localities provided rebates for real estate taxes. Henrico is the only one that also provided rebates for personal property. As it relates to restrictions of issuing rebates, the county would first have to adopt an ordinance.

Based on the statute, the return of surplus funds is limited to real estate and personal property taxes only, And refunds must be made to those who paid into the surplus for the given fiscal year. For real estate specifically, refunds would apply to both residential and commercial properties.

The surplus would have to be returned to the owners that were assessed taxes. And any ordinance drafted would have to set a date as of which ownership would be determined for the purposes of issuing a rebate. This would be a snapshot in time, such as the ownership as of the billing of the second installment real estate.

For personal property, the rebate would include both individual and business use vehicles and would also include business personal property. At this point, I will turn it over to Phil to run a few slides. Phil Hagen, Budget Director. So one of the things that we would need to talk about as we were to implement a rebate program would be the question of what defines a surplus because Virginia Code does not actually have a legal definition of what that surplus is. So we do have a bit of flexibility then and how we could define it. However, since the surplus is tied to either the real estate tax or personal property tax revenues, we think that a good option there

would be to look at the variance between actual receipts and the final revised budget for each of those taxes. We certainly think that would be a straightforward approach. In each of those cases, we would just be looking at the current year tax receipts and not looking at any of the delinquent collections from prior years. And so the chart on this slide gives those variances over a five-year period. You can see real estate, which is the blue bar, is very tight, under a quarter percent each year, and actually negative in this most recent year. Personal property tax variances are slightly higher. Of course, the overall tax base there is smaller, though. But even those are very close at

under two percent. So if we look at fiscal year 2026 as an example of what the impact would be, Again, our real estate tax variance was slightly negative, and so that would not allow for a potential rebate under this definition of what a surplus would be. Meanwhile, with personal property taxes, with a positive variance of $13.4 million, that could have allowed a rebate of about $11 per account, and that would include, again, both the individual and business personal property accounts. I would just note that $11 does not assume any administrative costs, and coming up

in a couple of slides, we have some options there on what the administrative cost would be. So we would certainly expect that actual rebate amount to be slightly lower than that $11 per account. Talking about the impact, though, if that $13 million in that personal property tax variance had been refunded to taxpayers, it would have impacted our carryover actions. And so we wanted to put this slide in here just to kind of give some context in that matter. Certainly the real estate and personal property tax variances aren't the sum total of what we have in balance at the end of the year. We have other tax categories that contribute to the revenue balance,

which was just over $63 million, this carryover. Some of the other categories that contributed to that balance were BPOL taxes, sales tax, investment earnings, as well as charges for services that all ran a little bit above what we had predicted. We also had savings of $107 million on the expenditure side of the ledger. And after prior year commitments, we had $106 million available for carryover adjustments.

And so we've provided the pie chart on this slide in order to show how those carryover funds were allocated. And certainly when we look at the largest categories on this pie chart where we have capital, IT, vehicle replacement, environmental and energy programs, those are categories where carryover funding really allows us to continue those programs.

That's where the bulk of the funding for those programs comes from. And without being able to dedicate carryover funding towards those items, we would be looking at needing to make additional baseline contributions into those. So certainly taking something that we need to take into account as we look at this, because we do have significant needs for carryover balances each year.

Turn it back to Greg. So what brings us to our options, based on our analysis, we really only have two options. Option one is the issuing of rebate checks. As you will see between the two, this one is more costly, and it would require the issuance of roughly one and a half million paper checks. That's 13 times more than our current annual operation at a total cost of $2.4 to $3.5 million, and it would require four new positions to manage the check printing process, as well as the return check and its achievement process.

The Department of Finance did look at outsourcing the check printing to Bank of America, but that would require the outsourcing of all check printing and would be at a total estimated cost of $3.5 million. From an IT development standpoint, since we do not presently have the ability to do rebates, a mass rebate in either of our tax systems, we're looking at an IT development timeline of anywhere from eight to nine months per tax type, and then there would be an additional 79 days required to process and mail the checks.

An alternative option would be to apply the rebate as a credit to future year tax accounts and issue rebate checks for those that have moved and or sold their property. With this option, we would still have to issue some rebate checks, but the volume of issuance would be lower at roughly $128,000 or double our current annual operations. The total estimated cost for this would be about a million dollars and one additional position. And then from an IT development standpoint, it would be similar to the issuing of the rebate checks. It would be eight to nine months per tax type, but the issuing of the checks

themselves would be reduced to roughly 13 days. And that concludes our presentation on tax rebates. Thank you for the presentation. I do think regardless of our opinion on this issue or not, we did just hear, I think, the reason why there are 95 counties in Virginia and 38 cities, and there are four jurisdictions in the entire Commonwealth of Virginia that have this program.

and I think we just heard why from my standpoint. But questions from board members. Supervisor Herity. Well, since this was my board matter, and thank you for doing the work, and I know it was a bit of work.

Just real quick on slide five, you were struggling with the definition of surplus. I mean, certainly surplus could be the, I mean, I think a valid definition would be projected revenues exceeding projected expenses.

It wouldn't have to be just a surplus on the revenue side, correct? Is there anything? So as I said here, certainly there is not a legal definition in Virginia Code. Okay. So we would have some flexibility. Got it. With the code being specific about returning real estate and personal property taxes, we certainly thought that looking at the variance of those two categories would be a straightforward way to go.

It is certainly open for other discussion about how that surplus could be defined. Do you know what other jurisdictions do, how they define it, just out of curiosity? Yeah, so they defined it like we define it here. They looked at the variances between the real estate and the personal property revenue and what was actually projected in their budget.

We met with Henrico County, and that's how they conveyed it to us as well. Okay. All right. I mean, and I certainly don't think we're going to see this in the near future, not with our deferred maintenance issues, our deferred IT issues, our pension liability issues, stagnant population.

What got me thinking about this is I did get a check from Louisa County, and it was a nice thing when you owned property down there and received a check. It's kind of an interesting mix of jurisdictions, and I know there's only four out of the 130-some jurisdictions there are in Virginia.

Interesting that only four did it. Louisa did it on real estate taxes, which was also interesting. But thank you very much. Obviously, if we get to the point we ever need to look at this, which I don't think is for the next several years, at least option two seemed to be the one that makes the most sense, but still a lot of work to do.

Did the option two include the IT cost of developing that, or was that? Yeah, that was included in the cost as well. It was included in it. Thank you. Okay, any other questions? Supervisor Stewart. This was, I think, very helpful for me to understand.

Obviously, the costs are significant, and if you did it, you'd want it to be enough dollars to offset the costs associated with it. I could see really one situation where it could be something we would consider, which is, you know, as we all know from the Weldon Cooper study, we send a dollar to Richmond and we get back 50 cents on the dollar.

If the state actually did start treating us more equitably here and we got 70%, 80% back, that kind of increase or largesse would be something we could in turn use to reduce our tax rate and or provide rebates to folks.

And I think that, to me, I would welcome that opportunity and welcome the fact that the state would actually treat us more equitably in Fairfax County and Northern Virginia in general. So thank you. Fair point, as always, consistent. Any other questions from board members on this?

Okay, we're going to move on to agenda item number three, which is Retirement Systems and Boards Consolidation Overview. Yes, we're going to have a change of personnel here at the table. So I'll ask to come to the table, our partners with PFM and Deep Blue Advisors, as well as we have a representative from each of the Retirement Boards of Trustees.

I will note that Jeff Weiler was supposed to be here to represent the retirement systems. However, he has a medical issue, and so he is not able to be here. I'm going to cover those slides for him, probably poorly. And if you guys have any specific questions about some of those items, I can take them back as budget Q&As.

So, Rich wants to come to the table. And Sean. Yep. So, we're going to start. This presentation is really divided up into two components. I'm going to cover the first number of slides, and then I'm going to pass it over to PFM and Deep Blue. So, the first two slides are really just to provide an overview.

I just don't mind passing me the remote. Thank you. But to provide an overview of the retirement systems, and so really just for folks listening, as a reminder, the county does have three separate retirement systems.

We have our employees' retirement system, which includes our general county employees. It also does include some employees from schools, those that are not in the Virginia retirement system, so food service workers, custodians, those are in our employees' retirement system. We have our Uniform Retirement System, which is primarily Uniform Fire and Rescue, Sheriff's Office, and Department of Public Safety Communications, and then we have our Police Officers Retirement System.

You can see in the chart here on the right, really just the scale of those systems. I mean, over $11 billion in assets when you combine the three. You can also see the most recent funded ratios for those systems, ranging anywhere from about 74% to just under 81%.

We look at our funding ratios on a more historical perspective. just look the past five years, you can see that those do fluctuate. This is based on market value of assets. So as the market changes, so do these funding ratios. They are also impacted by liability gains or losses, meaning how our experience compares in a given year compared to the assumptions that the actuaries have included in their valuations. And so you, again, can see that those funding ratios have fluctuated around mid-60s to a little above 80 percent.

We have had a lot of conversations with the bond rating agencies about our retirement systems. Some members of the board may recall a little more than a decade ago there were some concerns from the rating agencies regarding our pension funding, and so we put a number of guidelines into place to try to strengthen that.

The first was you can see there listed was amortizing 100 percent of the unfunded liability, that in our employer contribution rates. We were not doing that previously. We had a different funding method that we used. But since 2020, we have been amortizing 100% of the unfunded, including that in our employer contribution rates. So we did see an increase in employer contribution rates from about 2015 to about 2020, primarily as a result of this. The second tenet is in that until each system reaches 100% funding status, we will not reduce employer contributions for that system. Really, this comes into play, it's maybe come into play a handful of

times since we put this policy into place, where the actuaries has determined that we could reduce the employer contribution rate. We hold it steady. But the past couple of years, especially, we've seen contribution rates increase. So this guideline hasn't really come into play.
